question: Under Section 10-10(a), what must a licensee disclose to a client regarding the sponsoring broker's compensation?
choice_a: The sponsoring broker's compensation and policy with regard to cooperating with brokers who represent other parties in a transaction
choice_b: Only the total dollar amount of commission paid on the licensee's most recent closed transaction
choice_c: Nothing, unless the client submits a written request to the Department
choice_d: Only the compensation percentage stated in the multiple listing service data sheet
explanation: Section 10-10(a) requires a licensee to disclose to a client the sponsoring broker's compensation and policy regarding cooperating with brokers who represent other parties in the transaction.

question: Under Section 10-10(b), what must a licensee disclose to a client about compensation the licensee personally receives from a third party related to the transaction?
choice_a: All sources of compensation related to the transaction received by the licensee from a third party
choice_b: Only third-party compensation exceeding $1,000
choice_c: Only third-party compensation received after closing
choice_d: Nothing, since third-party compensation is the sponsoring broker's disclosure obligation, not the licensee's
explanation: Section 10-10(b) requires a licensee to disclose to a client all sources of compensation related to the transaction that the licensee receives from a third party.

question: Under Section 10-10(c), a licensee who refers a client to a business (other than a publicly traded company) must disclose an ownership interest in that business at what threshold, and when must the disclosure occur?
choice_a: An ownership interest greater than 1%, disclosed at the time the referral is made
choice_b: An ownership interest greater than 25%, disclosed within 10 business days after closing
choice_c: Any ownership interest at all, disclosed only if the client specifically asks
choice_d: An ownership interest greater than 50%, disclosed in the closing statement
explanation: Section 10-10(c) requires disclosure, at the time of making the referral, of an ownership interest greater than 1% (or receipt of profit distributions) in the entity to which the client is referred, with an exception for publicly traded companies.

question: Under Section 10-10(d), if a sponsoring broker receives compensation from both the buyer and seller (or lessee and lessor) in the same transaction, what must the broker do?
choice_a: Disclose in writing to a client the fact that compensation is being paid by both sides of the transaction
choice_b: Refund the smaller of the two compensation amounts to the party who paid less
choice_c: Obtain Department pre-approval before accepting compensation from either party
choice_d: Nothing further is required as long as both amounts are equal
explanation: Section 10-10(d) requires a sponsoring broker who receives compensation from both sides of a transaction to disclose that fact in writing to a client.

question: Does Section 10-10(e) permit an Illinois licensee to cooperate with and pay compensation to a broker licensed in another state or country?
choice_a: Yes, provided that broker complies with the licensing requirements of their own state or country
choice_b: No, cooperation and compensation are limited to brokers holding an active Illinois license
choice_c: Yes, but only through a reciprocal agreement filed with the Department in advance
choice_d: No, unless the out-of-state broker completes Illinois pre-license education first
explanation: Section 10-10(e) permits cooperation and compensation with brokers licensed in another state or country, provided they comply with their own jurisdiction's licensing requirements.

question: Under Section 10-15(a), may compensation be paid to an unlicensed person in exchange for that person performing activities that require a license under the Act?
choice_a: No, no compensation may be paid to an unlicensed person for performing licensed activities in violation of the Act
choice_b: Yes, so long as the payment is under $500
choice_c: Yes, so long as the unlicensed person discloses the payment to the Department within 30 days
choice_d: Yes, if the unlicensed person is a relative of the paying licensee
explanation: Section 10-15(a) prohibits paying compensation to an unlicensed person for performing licensed activities in violation of the Act.
source_note: Sec. 10-15(a), No compensation to persons in violation of Act.

question: Under Section 10-15(b), to maintain a court action to recover compensation for services that only a licensee could lawfully perform, what must have been true of the person at the time the service was performed?
choice_a: The person must have been duly licensed as a managing broker, broker, salesperson, or leasing agent under the Act at the time the act or service was performed
choice_b: The person need only obtain a license before filing the lawsuit
choice_c: The person must have been a member of the local Realtor association at the time of the service
choice_d: The person must have disclosed the unlicensed status to the client in writing
explanation: Section 10-15(b) bars a court action to recover compensation for licensed activities unless the person was duly licensed under the Act at the time the act or service was performed.
source_note: Sec. 10-15(b), No compensation to persons in violation of Act.

question: Under Section 10-15(c), may a licensee offer prizes, merchandise, rebates, or other consideration to an unlicensed person who is a party to a contract to buy, sell, or lease real estate?
choice_a: Yes, so long as the offer complies with subdivision (35) of subsection (a) of Section 20-20
choice_b: No, any such offer to a contracting party is prohibited outright
choice_c: Yes, but only if the consideration is cash rather than merchandise or rebates
choice_d: Yes, but only after the Department issues a case-by-case waiver
explanation: Section 10-15(c) permits a licensee to offer prizes, merchandise, services, rebates, discounts, or other consideration to an unlicensed party to a purchase, sale, or lease contract, so long as the offer complies with subdivision (35) of subsection (a) of Section 20-20.
source_note: Sec. 10-15(c), No compensation to persons in violation of Act.

question: Under Section 10-15(d), may a licensee offer cash, gifts, or chances to win a game of chance to a consumer to induce the consumer to use the licensee's services, even if a broker-client relationship never results?
choice_a: Yes, so long as the offer is not prohibited by any other law and complies with subdivision (35) of subsection (a) of Section 20-20
choice_b: No, such inducements may only be offered after a broker-client relationship is formed
choice_c: No, inducements to consumers are categorically prohibited under the Act
choice_d: Yes, but only if the value of the inducement is disclosed to the Department in advance
explanation: Section 10-15(d) permits a licensee to offer cash, gifts, prizes, awards, coupons, rebates, or chances to win a game of chance to a consumer as an inducement to use the licensee's services, even absent an eventual broker-client relationship, so long as not otherwise prohibited by law and compliant with subdivision (35) of subsection (a) of Section 20-20.
source_note: Sec. 10-15(d), No compensation to persons in violation of Act.

question: Under Section 10-15(e), may a licensee pay compensation to an unlicensed person who is not, and will not become, a party to a real estate transaction, in exchange for a referral of real estate services?
choice_a: No; a licensee who pays such a referral fee to an unlicensed non-party person is subject to discipline
choice_b: Yes, provided the referral fee is less than $500
choice_c: Yes, provided the unlicensed person is disclosed as a party on the closing statement
choice_d: Yes, without any restriction, since referral fees are not considered licensed activity
explanation: Section 10-15(e) prohibits paying compensation to an unlicensed person who is not and will not become a party to the transaction in exchange for a referral of real estate services; the Department's summary of Public Act 101-0357 identifies this as an express disciplinary basis under Section 10-15(e).
source_note: Sec. 10-15(e), No compensation to persons in violation of Act.

question: Does Section 10-15(f) waive or override the requirements of the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)?
choice_a: No; hedge: Section 10-15 is understood not to waive or abrogate RESPA's requirements, though the precise codified subsection letter for this savings clause was not independently re-verified against the official ILCS text
choice_b: Yes, Section 10-15 expressly supersedes RESPA for Illinois transactions
choice_c: Yes, but only for transactions involving federally related mortgage loans
choice_d: No, because RESPA does not apply to real estate brokerage compensation at all
explanation: Secondary sources describe Section 10-15 as including a savings clause stating that nothing in the Section waives or abrogates RESPA's provisions; this specific subsection lettering is flagged as a hedge since it could not be cross-checked against the official ilga.gov codified text during this research pass.
source_note: Sec. 10-15(f) (hedge: subsection lettering per secondary source, not independently confirmed against ilga.gov).

question: Under Section 15-25, what basic duty of honesty do licensees owe to customers (as opposed to clients)?
choice_a: To treat all customers honestly and not negligently or knowingly give them false information
choice_b: No duty of honesty is owed to a customer, only to a client
choice_c: A duty of honesty only if the customer is represented by an attorney
choice_d: A duty of honesty limited solely to statements made in writing
explanation: Section 15-25 requires licensees to treat all customers honestly and prohibits negligently or knowingly giving customers false information.

question: Under Section 15-25, a licensee engaged by a seller client must timely disclose which facts to a prospective-buyer customer?
choice_a: Latent material adverse facts about the property's physical condition that are actually known to the licensee and could not be discovered by the customer's reasonably diligent inspection
choice_b: All facts about the seller's personal financial motivation for selling
choice_c: The seller's original purchase price for the property
choice_d: Only facts that are already disclosed in the seller's written property disclosure form
explanation: Section 15-25 requires a licensee engaged by a seller client to timely disclose to buyer customers latent material adverse facts pertaining to the property's physical condition that are actually known to the licensee and could not be discovered by the customer's reasonably diligent inspection.

question: Under Section 15-25, is a licensee liable to a customer for passing along false information that the licensee's client supplied to the licensee?
choice_a: No, unless the licensee had actual knowledge that the information was false
choice_b: Yes, the licensee is strictly liable as a guarantor of all client-supplied information
choice_c: No, a licensee is never liable to a customer under any circumstances
choice_d: Yes, but only if the false information concerned the purchase price
explanation: Section 15-25 provides that a licensee is not liable to a customer for false information supplied by the licensee's client, unless the licensee had actual knowledge the information was false.

question: Under Section 15-25, may a cause of action arise against a licensee for revealing information in compliance with that Section's disclosure requirements?
choice_a: No, no cause of action shall arise against a licensee for revealing information in compliance with Section 15-25
choice_b: Yes, the customer may sue for any disclosure the customer finds unwelcome
choice_c: Yes, but only the licensee's own client may sue over the disclosure
choice_d: No, unless the disclosed information later proves inaccurate
explanation: Section 15-25 states that no cause of action shall arise against a licensee for revealing information in compliance with that Section.

question: Under Section 15-30, what happens to a broker's and licensee's duties to a client once a brokerage agreement terminates, expires, or is completed, absent a written agreement providing otherwise?
choice_a: No further duties are owed, except the duty to account for all moneys and property relating to the transaction
choice_b: All duties, including the duty to negotiate future offers, continue indefinitely
choice_c: All duties immediately end with no exceptions whatsoever
choice_d: Only the duty of loyalty continues, but the duty to account for money and property ends
explanation: Section 15-30 provides that after termination, expiration, or completion of a brokerage agreement, no further duties are owed to the client except as may be provided in a written agreement, subject to the duty to account for all moneys and property relating to the transaction.
source_note: Sec. 15-30, Duties owed by a broker or licensee after termination, expiration, or completion of brokerage agreement.

question: Under Section 15-30, besides accounting for money and property, what other duty survives the termination, expiration, or completion of a brokerage agreement?
choice_a: The duty to keep confidential all confidential information received during the course of the brokerage agreement
choice_b: The duty to continue marketing the property at no additional cost
choice_c: The duty to represent the same client in any future transaction
choice_d: The duty to notify the client's competitors of the termination
explanation: Section 15-30 provides that, along with the duty to account for moneys and property, the duty to keep confidential all confidential information received during the brokerage agreement survives its termination, expiration, or completion.
source_note: Sec. 15-30, Duties owed by a broker or licensee after termination, expiration, or completion of brokerage agreement.

question: Under Section 15-35(a), by when must a licensee acting as a designated agent advise a consumer in writing of the designated agency relationship (absent a different written agreement)?
choice_a: No later than before beginning work as the consumer's designated agent
choice_b: Any time before closing, at the licensee's discretion
choice_c: Only if the consumer specifically requests it in writing
choice_d: Within 30 days after the brokerage agreement is signed
explanation: Section 15-35(a) requires a licensee acting as a designated agent to advise the consumer in writing of the designated agency relationship no later than before beginning work as the designated agent, unless a different relationship is documented in a written agreement between the sponsoring broker and the consumer.

question: Under Section 15-35(a), the written disclosure identifying the designated agent(s) may appear where, and what recordkeeping does it require?
choice_a: In the brokerage agreement or a separate document, with a copy retained by the broker and a copy provided to the consumer
choice_b: Only in a standalone document filed with the Department within 10 days
choice_c: Only within the multiple listing service data sheet for the property
choice_d: Verbally is sufficient, with no written copy required for either party
explanation: Section 15-35(a) allows the designated agency disclosure, which must name the designated agent(s), to be part of the brokerage agreement or a separate document, with the broker retaining a copy and providing a copy to the consumer.

question: Under Section 15-35(c), when must a licensee who is NOT acting as a customer's agent provide written disclosure of that fact to the customer?
choice_a: At a time intended to prevent disclosure of confidential information, but no later than when preparing an offer to purchase or lease property
choice_b: At closing, as part of the settlement statement
choice_c: Only if the customer later files a complaint with the Department
choice_d: There is no disclosure requirement for non-agency relationships with customers
explanation: Section 15-35(c) requires a licensee not acting as a customer's agent to provide written disclosure of that fact at a time intended to prevent disclosure of confidential information, and in no event later than when preparing an offer to purchase or lease.

question: Under Section 15-40, does the payment or promise of payment of compensation to a licensee, by itself, establish that an agency relationship has been created with a consumer?
choice_a: No, payment or promise of compensation is not determinative of whether an agency relationship has been created
choice_b: Yes, any payment automatically creates an agency relationship as a matter of law
choice_c: Yes, but only if the payment exceeds the customary commission rate
choice_d: No agency relationship can ever be created by a compensation arrangement
explanation: Section 15-40 states that the payment or promise of payment of compensation to a licensee is not determinative of whether an agency relationship has been created between the licensee and a consumer.
source_note: Sec. 15-40, Compensation does not determine agency relationship.

question: A buyer pays Licensee X a transaction fee at closing, but the buyer never signed a buyer brokerage agreement or otherwise agreed to be represented by Licensee X. Under Section 15-40, does that payment, standing alone, make Licensee X the buyer's agent?
choice_a: No; under Section 15-40, receiving compensation does not by itself determine that an agency relationship exists
choice_b: Yes, accepting any payment from a consumer automatically creates agency by operation of law
choice_c: Yes, but only because the payment was made at closing rather than earlier
choice_d: No, because only sponsoring brokers, not sponsored licensees, can ever be deemed agents
explanation: Applying Section 15-40, compensation received from a consumer does not by itself determine whether an agency relationship was created; agency depends on the parties' agreement and conduct, not merely on who paid a fee.
source_note: Sec. 15-40, Compensation does not determine agency relationship.

question: Under Section 15-45(a), under what condition may an individual licensee, or a sponsoring broker's licensees, act as a dual agent in the same transaction?
choice_a: Only with the informed written consent of all clients, obtained on a disclosure form explaining the conflict of interest and what a dual agent may and may not disclose
choice_b: Automatically, whenever the same brokerage represents both the buyer and the seller
choice_c: Only with the Department's prior written approval of the specific transaction
choice_d: Only if both clients are represented by separate attorneys throughout the transaction
explanation: Section 15-45(a) permits dual agency (by an individual licensee, or by one or more of a sponsoring broker's licensees in the same transaction) only with the informed written consent of all clients, using a disclosure form addressing the conflict of interest and permitted/prohibited disclosures.

question: Under Section 15-45(b), when must the dual agency disclosure form be presented to a client, and when may it be signed?
choice_a: It must be presented at the time the brokerage agreement is entered into, though it may be signed any time before dual agency actually occurs
choice_b: It must be both presented and signed only at the closing table
choice_c: It need not be presented until after dual agency has already begun
choice_d: It must be presented within 24 hours after an offer is accepted
explanation: Section 15-45(b) requires the dual agency disclosure form to be presented at the time the brokerage agreement is entered into, though it may be signed at any time before the dual agency relationship actually occurs.

question: Under Section 15-45(c), before execution of an offer or contract, what must a licensee obtain from clients who previously consented to dual agency?
choice_a: A written confirmation of the prior dual agency consent, which may be included within the purchase or lease agreement itself
choice_b: A new notarized affidavit filed with the county recorder
choice_c: Nothing further; the original disclosure form alone suffices for every future transaction
choice_d: A verbal reaffirmation witnessed by the sponsoring broker
explanation: Section 15-45(c) requires a written confirmation of the clients' prior consent to dual agency before execution of an offer or contract, which confirmation may be included within the purchase or lease agreement.

question: Under Section 15-45(d), is a dual agent subject to a cause of action for making disclosures that are permitted or required under the Act's dual agency provisions?
choice_a: No, a dual agent faces no cause of action for making disclosures permitted or required under those provisions
choice_b: Yes, any disclosure to one client about the other client's position is automatically actionable
choice_c: Yes, unless the disclosure is approved in advance by the Department
choice_d: No, but only for disclosures made in writing rather than verbally
explanation: Section 15-45(d) shields a dual agent from a cause of action for making disclosures that are permitted or required under the Article's dual agency provisions.

question: Under Section 15-45(e), in a dual agency relationship, is knowledge held by one client, or by that client's broker, automatically imputed to the other client or broker?
choice_a: No, there is no imputation of knowledge or information among or between clients, brokers, or their affiliated licensees
choice_b: Yes, all knowledge held by either side is automatically imputed to the other under dual agency
choice_c: Yes, but only knowledge relating to the purchase price is imputed
choice_d: No, unless the two clients share the same attorney
explanation: Section 15-45(e) provides that in dual agency there is no imputation of knowledge or information among or between clients, brokers, or their affiliated licensees.

question: Under Section 15-45(f), if a client refuses to consent to dual agency, may the licensee withdraw from representing that client without prejudicing the representation of the other client in the transaction?
choice_a: Yes, the licensee may withdraw from representing the non-consenting client without prejudicing representation of the other client
choice_b: No, withdrawal from either client automatically terminates the representation of both
choice_c: No, a licensee may never withdraw from a client relationship once a brokerage agreement is signed
choice_d: Yes, but only if the sponsoring broker personally takes over both clients' representation
explanation: Section 15-45(f) allows a licensee to withdraw from representing a client who does not consent to dual agency without prejudicing the representation of the other client.

question: Under Section 15-45(f), if a licensee who withdrew from representing one client in a dual agency scenario later receives a referral fee connected to that client, what must occur?
choice_a: The referral fee must be disclosed to both parties
choice_b: The referral fee must be forfeited entirely to the Real Estate Recovery Fund
choice_c: No disclosure of the referral fee is required to either party
choice_d: The referral fee must be disclosed only to the client who did not consent to dual agency
explanation: Section 15-45(f) requires that a referral fee received in connection with a client from whom the licensee withdrew in a dual agency scenario be disclosed to both parties.

question: Under Section 15-45(g), may a licensee serve as a dual agent in a transaction where the licensee, or an entity in which the licensee has or will have an ownership interest, is itself a party to the transaction?
choice_a: No, a licensee shall not serve as a dual agent in that circumstance
choice_b: Yes, provided both other parties give informed written consent
choice_c: Yes, as long as the licensee's ownership interest is under 10%
choice_d: Yes, provided the sponsoring broker personally supervises the transaction
explanation: Section 15-45(g) prohibits a licensee from serving as a dual agent in any transaction where the licensee, or an entity in which the licensee has or will have an ownership interest, is a party to the transaction.

question: Under Section 15-50(a-5), if a client and a licensee never signed a written brokerage agreement, does the absence of that writing automatically defeat the client's ability to enforce an oral brokerage agreement or to establish that licensed activity occurred?
choice_a: No, subsection (a-5) preserves enforcement of oral agreements, and the absence of a writing is not by itself a defense to whether an agreement existed or licensed activity occurred; courts retain authority to impose legal or equitable remedies
choice_b: Yes, an oral brokerage agreement is automatically void and unenforceable under all circumstances
choice_c: Yes, but only if the transaction involved commercial rather than residential property
choice_d: No, but only equitable remedies (never legal remedies) are available for an unwritten agreement
explanation: Section 15-50(a-5) states that the section does not prevent a client from enforcing an oral brokerage agreement, and that the absence of a written agreement is not, by itself, a defense to whether an agreement existed or whether licensed activity occurred; courts retain authority to grant legal or equitable remedies.

question: Under Section 15-50(b), what duty does a sponsoring broker owe with respect to confidential information a client discloses to a designated agent?
choice_a: To take ordinary and necessary care to protect that confidential information
choice_b: No duty at all, since only the designated agent (not the sponsoring broker) is bound by confidentiality
choice_c: A duty to immediately share the information with all other licensees in the office
choice_d: A duty to forward the information to the Department for recordkeeping
explanation: Section 15-50(b) requires a sponsoring broker to take ordinary and necessary care to protect confidential information disclosed by a client to a designated agent.

question: Under Section 15-50(c), may a designated agent share a client's confidential information with the sponsoring broker or other specified persons, and what limit applies to further disclosure by the broker?
choice_a: Yes, for the purpose of obtaining advice that benefits the client regarding a potential transaction, but the broker may not further disclose the information unless required by law or permitted by the client
choice_b: No, a designated agent may never share client confidential information with anyone, including the sponsoring broker
choice_c: Yes, and the sponsoring broker may then freely disclose it to any other licensee in the brokerage without restriction
choice_d: Yes, but only after the transaction has closed
explanation: Section 15-50(c) allows a designated agent to share client confidential information with the sponsoring broker or other specified persons for advice benefiting the client regarding a potential transaction, while limiting the broker's further disclosure of that information absent legal requirement or client permission.

question: Under Section 15-65, does the agency-relationship framework of Article 15 limit the Department's authority to regulate licensees under other Articles of the Act?
choice_a: No, nothing in Article 15 limits the Department's regulation under other Articles, and the Department may adopt rules necessary to implement and enforce Article 15
choice_b: Yes, Article 15 fully displaces the Department's disciplinary authority under all other Articles
choice_c: Yes, but only with respect to advertising violations
choice_d: No, but the Department may not adopt any new rules specific to Article 15
explanation: Section 15-65 provides that nothing in Article 15 limits the Department's regulation of licensees under the Act's other Articles, and authorizes the Department to adopt rules necessary for Article 15's implementation and enforcement.

question: Under Section 15-70(a), in an action brought under Article 15, what remedies may a court award, in its discretion?
choice_a: Only actual damages and court costs, or injunctive relief when appropriate
choice_b: Punitive damages up to three times the actual damages
choice_c: Mandatory attorney's fees regardless of the outcome
choice_d: Rescission of the transaction as the sole available remedy
explanation: Section 15-70(a) limits a court's discretionary award in an Article 15 action to actual damages and court costs, or injunctive relief when appropriate.

question: Under Section 15-70(b), within how many years after a person knew or should reasonably have known of the act or omission must an Article 15 action generally be commenced?
choice_a: 2 years
choice_b: 1 year
choice_c: 4 years
choice_d: 6 years
explanation: Section 15-70(b) bars an Article 15 action unless commenced within 2 years after the person bringing the action knew or should reasonably have known of the act or omission.

question: Under Section 15-70(b), regardless of when the act or omission was discovered, an Article 15 action may in no event be brought more than how many years after the act or omission occurred?
choice_a: 5 years
choice_b: 2 years
choice_c: 10 years
choice_d: 3 years
explanation: Section 15-70(b) provides an absolute outer limit: an Article 15 action may in no event be brought more than 5 years after the date the act or omission occurred.

question: Under Section 15-70(b), if the person entitled to bring an Article 15 action is under 18 years of age or under a legal disability, when does the limitations period begin to run?
choice_a: Not until the disability (minority or legal disability) is removed
choice_b: It begins to run on the date of the act or omission regardless of age or disability
choice_c: It begins to run once the person's parent or guardian is notified in writing
choice_d: The limitations period is waived entirely for a person under a legal disability
explanation: Section 15-70(b) tolls the limitations period for a person under 18 or under legal disability until the disability is removed, at which point the period begins to run.
